Inherited from Old Norse gaumr (“heed, attention”), from Proto-Germanic *gaumaz (“heed, attention”). The further origin is disputed. The word has traditionally been connected with Old Norse gá (“to notice, perceive”), though this connection has been questioned in more recent Germanic etymology.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk gaum, Icelandic gaumur and gaum, Old English ġīeme and ġȳme, Old Frisian gāme, Old Saxon gōma and Old High German gouma (“heed, attention”). English gaum (“heed, attention”) was borrowed through Middle English from Old Norse.

104.etyen:
Unadapted borrowing from Italian a cappella (“in the manner of the chapel; in church style”), literally “in the chapel”. Italian a (“to, at, in”) is from Latin ad (“to, towards, at”), from Proto-Italic *ad (“toward, to, at”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“near, at”). Italian cappella (“chapel; church choir”) is from Latin cappella (“little cloak; chapel”), a diminutive of cappa (“cloak, cape”), of disputed origin.
The musical expression originally meant “as in the chapel, in church style”, referring to the practice of church choirs.
Compare the parallel borrowings Danish a cappel

1000040.etyen:
Internationalism, based on Rwanda-Rundi Burundi (“Burundi”), a class 14 proper noun in the Kirundi variety of Rwanda-Rundi. The name is conventionally analysed as the class-14 prefix bu- and the stem -rundi, approximately “land of the Rundi people”; the deeper origin of the stem is uncertain.
Parallel international adaptations include Norwegian Nynorsk Burundi, Danish Burundi, Swedish Burundi, German Burundi, Dutch Burundi and English Burundi.

1000552.etyen:
Borrowed from Arabic مُحَمَّد (muḥammad, “praised, commendable”), the passive participle of Arabic حَمَّدَ (ḥammada, “to praise, commend”), from the root ح م د (ḥ-m-d, “praise”).
Related Arabic names include أَحْمَد (ʔaḥmad, “more praiseworthy”) and مَحْمُود (maḥmūd, “praised”).

en.g: pah, pooh, pfui; used to reproduce a blowing sound from the lips expressing contempt, scorn or mockery
x: pfui for et pak –, kom mig ikke for nær, I dumfødte dårer, som håber og tror at eie den hele umulige jord
Pfui, what a rabble — don't come near me, you foolish idiots who hope and believe you own the whole impossible earth.

1000808.etyen:
Onomatopoeic, imitating a blowing sound made with the lips and used as an expression of contempt or mockery.
Compare German pfui (“ugh, fie”), Danish pfuj (“ugh, fie”), English pfui, French pfui (“ugh, fie”) and Latin phui (“ugh, fie”). These expressive forms are ultimately sound-symbolic, so their exact historical relationships are not always clear.

1004392.etyen:
From Nord (“north”) + Makedonia (“Macedonia”), corresponding to Macedonian Северна Македонија (Severna Makedonija, “North Macedonia”). The country adopted the name officially on 12 February 2019, when the Prespa Agreement entered into force.
The second element is ultimately from Ancient Greek Μᾰκεδονῐ́ᾱ (Măkedonĭ́ā, “Macedonia”), from Μᾰκεδών (Măkedṓn, “Macedonian”) and the place-name suffix -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā). The name is traditionally associated with μᾰκεδνός (măkednós, “high, tall”) and the idea of a highland.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Nord-Makedonia, Danish Nordmakedonien, Swedish Nordmakedonien,

1005160.etyen:
Compound of hvitløk (“garlic”) + brød (“bread”), literally “garlic bread”.
Within the first element, hvit (“white”) continues Old Norse hvítr (“white”), from Proto-Germanic *hwītaz (“white”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱweyt- (“to shine”), while løk (“onion”) continues Old Norse laukr (“leek, onion, garlic”), from Proto-Germanic *laukaz (“leek, onion”), of uncertain further origin.
The second element goes back to Old Norse brauð (“bread”), from Proto-Germanic *braudą (“bread”). NAOB identifies the written form with Danish brød (“bread”), from Old Danish brøth (“bread”).
